questions.q: State the frequency range of microwaves used in terrestrial communication and name the propagation mode they primarily use.
questions.a: Microwaves: 300 MHz – 300 GHz (commonly 1–40 GHz for terrestrial links). Propagation: Line-of-sight (space wave). A wrong answer like "microwaves use sky wave propagation" reveals confusion between HF radio (3–30 MHz) which reflects off ionosphere, and microwaves which penetrate ionosphere and require direct visibility between antennas.

questions.q: A student claims: "Satellite communication uses radio waves, so it's just another type of radio transmission — no need to study it separately." Explain why this is incorrect by comparing propagation, latency, and infrastructure.
questions.a: While both use EM waves, satellite links differ critically: (1) Propagation: radio (ground/sky wave) follows Earth/ionosphere; satellite uses space wave (direct LOS to orbit). (2) Latency: GEO satellite ≈ 240 ms one-way (72,000 km round-trip); terrestrial radio ≈ negligible. (3) Infrastructure: radio uses ground towers; satellite needs launch, transponders, earth stations. Treating them as same ignores these design-impacting differences. A wrong answer that only mentions "both wireless" misses the engineering distinction.

questions.q: A company needs to connect two offices 40 km apart in hilly terrain where laying fiber is impossible. They consider: (a) UHF radio (500 MHz), (b) Microwave link (6 GHz), (c) LEO satellite. Which option is most suitable and why? Justify with propagation characteristics.
questions.a: Microwave (6 GHz) is best. UHF (500 MHz) at 40 km in hills suffers diffraction loss and multipath fading; requires tall towers. LEO satellite adds 20–40 ms latency, expensive terminals, handover complexity. Microwave at 6 GHz: LOS achievable with 30–40 m towers on hilltops, 30–50 km repeater spacing matches 40 km, high bandwidth (100s Mbps–Gbps), low latency (~0.13 ms). A wrong choice of UHF ignores terrain blockage; LEO ignores cost/latency for short distance.

questions.q: Compare the bandwidth-distance trade-off for terrestrial microwave vs GEO satellite. Why can microwave achieve higher data rates over 50 km than GEO satellite over 36,000 km, despite both using similar frequency bands (e.g., 6/4 GHz C-band)?
questions.a: Microwave: short distance (50 km) → low free-space path loss (~140 dB), high SNR, allows high-order modulation (256-QAM) → 1–10 Gbps. GEO satellite: 36,000 km → path loss ~200 dB, low SNR, limited by transponder power/bandwidth (36 MHz typical) → 10–100 Mbps per transponder. Also satellite shares bandwidth among many users. Same frequency, but distance^2 path loss and power constraints make satellite bandwidth-distance product far worse. Wrong answer citing only "satellite is far" misses the quantitative link budget impact.

questions.q: Evaluate this statement for a board exam answer: "Infrared waves are used for satellite communication because they have very high frequency and hence high bandwidth." Is it correct? Defend your evaluation.
questions.a: Incorrect. Satellite communication uses radio/microwave bands (L/S/C/Ku/Ka band: 1–40 GHz), NOT infrared (300 GHz–400 THz). Infrared cannot penetrate atmosphere (absorbed by water vapor, CO2) and is used only for short-range LOS (TV remotes, IrDA). High frequency ≠ usable for satellite; atmospheric windows matter. A student writing this confuses "high frequency = high bandwidth" (true in principle) with "any high frequency works" (false — propagation physics dominates). Board answer must name actual satellite bands (e.g., Ku: 14/12 GHz uplink/downlink).

questions.q: Design a wireless connectivity plan for a disaster relief camp in a remote valley (no cellular, no fiber). You have: HF radio (10 MHz), VHF radio (150 MHz), microwave (5 GHz), and a portable VSAT (Ku-band). Specify which technology for: (a) camp-to-HQ 500 km, (b) intra-camp 200 m, (c) camp-to-nearby-village 15 km (LOS blocked by ridge). Justify each choice.
questions.a: (a) HF radio (10 MHz) — sky wave via ionosphere reaches 500 km beyond horizon; low bandwidth but works without infrastructure. (b) VHF (150 MHz) or Wi-Fi (2.4/5 GHz) — short range, LOS not needed at 200 m, easy deployment. (c) VSAT (Ku-band) — satellite bypasses ridge; microwave blocked by ridge (no LOS), VHF/HF unreliable for data at 15 km in valley. A poor answer uses microwave for (c) ignoring ridge blockage, or VSAT for (b) wasting cost/latency.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Unguided transmission media (wireless media) transmit ______ signals through air, vacuum, or water without a physical conductor, using radio waves (30 Hz–300 GHz), microwaves (300 MHz–300 GHz), and infrared/satellite links, where propagation occurs via ground wave, sky wave, line-of-sight, or space wave modes depending on frequency and antenna configuration.

Fill in the blank: Imagine you're streaming a live cricket match from Mumbai to a village in Ladakh — the signal travels from the stadium camera to a ______ 36,000 km above the equator, then down to a dish antenna on a rooftop in Leh.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can: (1) Classify unguided media by frequency band and propagation mode with correct frequency ranges; (2) Explain why microwave links require line-of-sight and repeaters every 30–50 km; (3) Calculate satellite link latency for GEO vs LEO orbits and identify applications suited to each; (4) Compare bandwidth, attenuation, and.
